teaching.causalExplanation: This dot point has two halves. The first is drugs in injury management: painkillers, anti-inflammatories, which reduce swelling and pain, local anaesthetic injections that numb an area, and cortisone injections, which close to competition need an exemption. They're mostly legal, often prescribed, and used at every level of sport. The second is drugs taken to improve performance, many of them banned. The first affects far more athletes. Its central risk is masking: removing the pain signal without removing the damage. Pain is information. It tells you a tissue isn't coping with the load. Switch it off and keep playing, and a minor injury can become a serious one, with no banned substance at all. Pain relief still has a place, in sleep and rehab. The question is whether a drug is supporting recovery, or letting them ignore the injury. The performance substances are best learned by category, each with a mechanism. Anabolic agents build muscle and speed recovery, but raise blood pressure, upset blood fats, damage the liver and disrupt hormones. Stimulants raise alertness and hide fatigue, but push heart rate and blood pressure up, can trigger abnormal heart rhythms, and impair cooling, so heat illness becomes a real risk mid-game. Blood doping and hormones that boost red blood cells raise oxygen carrying, but thicken the blood, raising the risk of clots and stroke, worse when dehydrated. Beta blockers steady the heart and hands in precision sports like archery, but can drop heart rate and blood pressure too far. Notice that many of these risks are worst during exercise. And for teenagers, still growing, hormonal agents carry extra risks. Now ethics, and each argument needs its reply. Fairness: sport compares athletes under shared conditions, and a hidden advantage changes what the result means. The reply is that sport is already unequal, in money, coaching and technology, as you saw earlier. The answer: the problem isn't inequality as such, but a concealed and harmful advantage. And the strongest argument: coercion. If doping works and goes undetected, every other athlete faces a choice: dope too, or lose. So "it's my body, my choice" misses the point, because the choice doesn't stay with one person. Back to the hook. Only the stimulant is unfair to rivals. But both override a warning signal, and the painkiller may well cause more harm.

scenes.teachingReason: This dot point has two halves. The first is drugs in injury management: painkillers, anti-inflammatories, which reduce swelling and pain, local anaesthetic injections that numb an area, and cortisone injections, which close to competition need an exemption. They're mostly legal, often prescribed, and used at every level of sport. The second is drugs taken to improve performance, many of them banned. The first affects far more athletes. Its central risk is masking: removing the pain signal without removing the damage. Pain is information. It tells you a tissue isn't coping with the load. Switch it off and keep playing, and a minor injury can become a serious one, with no banned substance at all. Pain relief still has a place, in sleep and rehab. The question is whether a drug is supporting recovery, or letting them ignore the injury.

scenes.teachingReason: The performance substances are best learned by category, each with a mechanism. Anabolic agents build muscle and speed recovery, but raise blood pressure, upset blood fats, damage the liver and disrupt hormones. Stimulants raise alertness and hide fatigue, but push heart rate and blood pressure up, can trigger abnormal heart rhythms, and impair cooling, so heat illness becomes a real risk mid-game. Blood doping and hormones that boost red blood cells raise oxygen carrying, but thicken the blood, raising the risk of clots and stroke, worse when dehydrated. Beta blockers steady the heart and hands in precision sports like archery, but can drop heart rate and blood pressure too far. Notice that many of these risks are worst during exercise. And for teenagers, still growing, hormonal agents carry extra risks.

scenes.teachingReason: Now ethics, and each argument needs its reply. Fairness: sport compares athletes under shared conditions, and a hidden advantage changes what the result means. The reply is that sport is already unequal, in money, coaching and technology, as you saw earlier. The answer: the problem isn't inequality as such, but a concealed and harmful advantage. And the strongest argument: coercion. If doping works and goes undetected, every other athlete faces a choice: dope too, or lose. So "it's my body, my choice" misses the point, because the choice doesn't stay with one person. Back to the hook. Only the stimulant is unfair to rivals. But both override a warning signal, and the painkiller may well cause more harm.

scenes.teachingReason: Drug testing has several working parts. A prohibited list, updated every year, with some substances banned at all times and others only in competition. Testing out of competition, without notice, because many drugs are used in training and cleared before the event. Each sample is split into A and B, so one lab error can't end a career. Strict liability, from earlier: the athlete is responsible for whatever is in their sample, however it got there, because intent can't be proven. But testing has limits. A test only finds what it's designed to find, so new substances go undetected. Small, repeated doses can stay under detection limits. And so a negative test doesn't prove an athlete is clean.

If you're unsure about any medicine or supplement, ask a doctor or a sports dietitian.
